result.summary: Jove forbids the gods to help either side, then tips the scales toward the Trojans. Hector drives the Achaeans behind their wall, Juno and Minerva are turned back by Iris, and night stops the Trojans, who camp on the plain.

scenes.title: Jove's council and threat
scenes.summary: Jove warns the gods not to interfere and boasts of his strength with the golden chain. He then drives to Ida to watch the battle.
scenes.stakes: The gods risk being thrown into Tartarus if they defy Jove.

scenes.title: Scales tip; Nestor rescued
scenes.summary: Jove weighs the fates and thunders. Diomed saves Nestor, kills Eniopeus, and is turned back by Jove's thunderbolt while Hector taunts him.
scenes.stakes: Nestor could be killed, and the Achaeans face rout.

scenes.title: Juno urges Neptune
scenes.summary: Juno shakes with rage and urges Neptune to help the Danaans. He refuses to oppose Jove.
scenes.stakes: Defying Jove would bring his wrath.

scenes.title: Agamemnon's prayer; Teucer's bow
scenes.summary: Agamemnon prays and Jove sends an eagle. The Achaeans rally, and Teucer shoots many Trojans until Hector stones him.
scenes.stakes: The Achaean ships are about to be burned.

scenes.title: Goddesses turned back by Iris
scenes.summary: Hector drives the Achaeans to their ships. Juno and Minerva set out to help but Iris delivers Jove's threat. Jove tells Juno that Hector will fight on until Patroclus dies.
scenes.stakes: The goddesses risk lightning and injury from Jove.

scenes.title: Night and Trojan watchfires
scenes.summary: Night falls. Hector holds council, orders watchfires, and sacrifices are made. A thousand fires burn on the plain.
scenes.stakes: Hector fears the Achaeans may escape by night, losing his chance at victory.

notable_quotes.reason: Jove's golden chain boast, a famous image of divine supremacy.
Celebrated simile of the Trojan watchfires like stars.
Nestor states that no man can thwart Jove's purpose.

analysis.text: Jove's supremacy and the fixed course of fate dominate the book. Even the gods must yield to his plan to honour Achilles.
The weighing of fates and the golden chain reflect early Greek ideas of destiny tied to the king of the gods.

legacy.text: Jove's golden chain became a long-used image of the chain of being in later literature.

fun_facts.text: The Hours guard the gates of heaven in this book, an unusual role for them.

language_notes.text: "Clad in her robe of saffron" is a stock description of Dawn (Morning) as a goddess wearing saffron-yellow, the colour of sunrise.
"Inordinately" means excessively or beyond measure; "ere" means before.
Tartarus is the deepest part of the underworld, a prison for defeated gods such as the Titans, far below Hades, the realm of the dead.
"Hangs me a golden chain" is an archaic imperative: "Hang a golden chain for me." "Into the bargain" means in addition.
"Gainsaid" means denied or contradicted; Minerva says Jove's power cannot be disputed.
"Trito-born" is an epithet of Minerva, of uncertain origin, linked to Lake Triton or a river Triton.
"Nothing loth" means not unwilling, that is, eagerly. "Twixt" is short for "betwixt", meaning between.
"The sire of all" means Jove, father of gods and men. His golden scales weigh the two sides' fates of death to show who will lose.
"Servants of Mars" means warriors devoted to Mars (the Greek Ares), god of war. The two Ajaxes are the Greek champions Ajax son of Telamon and Ajax son of Oileus.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris, the Trojan prince who carried off Helen and so caused the war.
The horses of Tros were descended from the stock Jove gave Tros, an early king of Troy. Diomed captured them from Aeneas.
"Vouchsafes" means graciously grants or allows.
Hector refers to the honours a warrior received at feasts: the best seat, portions of meat and full cups. He says Diomed will lose them.
"Thrice did he doubt" uses the Homeric habit of repeating an action three times for emphasis.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) was the smith god who made armour for heroes. Diomed's cuirass is divine work, so it is a great prize.
"Vaunt" means boast; Jove (the Greek Zeus) has just been boasting of his power over the other gods.
Helice and Aegae were towns in Achaea where Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) was worshipped, so the Danaans' offerings there are in his honour.
"Pent up" means shut in, confined.
Refers to boasting feasts held on Lemnos, a stop on the Greeks' voyage to Troy.
"Vouchsafe" means graciously grant.
"Hie" means hurry.
"Meed" means reward or prize; "Ilius" is another name for Troy.
"His wrist was less" means his wrist lost its strength and could no longer grip.
Gorgo is the Gorgon, a monster whose terrible glare was said to petrify those who met it. Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war.
Danaans, like Achaeans and Argives, is a name for the Greeks. Aegis-bearing refers to Jove's aegis, a goatskin shield or cape that inspires terror.
His son is Hercules. Eurystheus, king of Argos, set him twelve labours, which Minerva here says she helped him survive.
The hell-hound is Cerberus, who guarded the underworld. Fetching him was Hercules' last labour. Erebus is the dark region of the dead, and Styx a river there.
Thetis, mother of Achilles, begged Jove in Book 1 to honour her son by letting the Trojans prevail. Touching knee and beard was the formal gesture of a suppliant.
Gold-bedizened means gaudily or richly decked with gold.
The Hours are goddesses of the seasons. Here they act as gatekeepers of Olympus, opening and closing the clouds.
The lord of the earthquake is Neptune (the Greek Poseidon), whose usual epithet it is. Here he serves Jove as groom.
Jove foretells that Hector will keep fighting until Achilles, the son of Peleus, rejoins the war over the body of Patroclus, which is the turning point of the poem.
Tartarus is the deepest pit of the underworld, where the defeated Titans Iapetus and Saturn are imprisoned.
Oceanus is the great river thought to encircle the world; the sun was imagined to set into it and rise from it.
A cubit is about the length of a forearm, roughly 18 inches, so the spear is around 16 feet long: an extraordinary weapon.
Ilius is another name for Troy, used throughout this translation.
"Take a dart with him to nurse at home" means each fleeing Achaean would carry a wound home with him.
"Scatheless" means unharmed.
"Fate-sped hounds" calls the Achaeans dogs driven by fate to Troy; Hector says the fates, not their strength, brought them.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I expect."
A hecatomb was a large sacrifice, originally of a hundred oxen, offered to the gods.

context_notes.text: Achaeans, Danaans and Argives are all names Homer uses for the Greeks. Here Jove stops the gods from helping either side.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) favours the Greeks. Jove is her father, so her reply is respectful but shows her sympathy for them.
Ida is the mountain near Troy where Jove watches the war, and Gargarus is its highest peak, sacred to him.
Mount Ida, near Troy, is where Jove sits to watch the battle. He had forbidden the other gods to help either side.
Nestor, king of Gerene, is the oldest Achaean leader, respected for his wisdom. His age makes him vulnerable in this fast chariot fighting.
Brimstone is sulphur. Its smell was associated with lightning, and here it marks the thunderbolt as a sign of Jove's will.
Andromache is Hector's wife, daughter of Eetion, a king killed by Achilles. Horses of the time were fed grain and sometimes wine.
Neptune is god of the sea and earthquakes; hence the title "lord of the earthquake."
Eagles were Jove's bird, and their flight was read as an omen. The fawn dropped at his altar signals divine favour.
Teucer was Telamon's illegitimate son, half-brother of Ajax, which explains the remark about his being a bastard.
Mount Ida, near Troy, is where Jove sits to watch the battle. Iris is the gods' winged messenger.
Juno is Jove's wife and often opposes him. Minerva, his daughter, is the one he threatens most harshly here.
Dardanians are Trojans descended from Dardanus, ancestor of the Trojan royal line; they are named separately from the allies.
Diomed (Diomedes), son of Tydeus, is the Achaean hero who has been fighting most fiercely against the Trojans.
Fifty men to a fire, times a thousand fires, gives fifty thousand men, an epic exaggeration of the Trojan army.

literary_notes.text: The image of hauling up all the gods, earth and sea on one chain exaggerates Jove's strength to make his supremacy clear.
The gods' frightened silence shows Jove's authority, while Minerva's careful, dutiful reply shows her tact and her loyalties.
Jove's smiling claim that he is not in earnest softens his threat, showing his affection for Minerva despite the harsh words.
Hiding the horses in a cloud and Jove sitting glorious on the peaks creates a remote, watchful figure above the war.
The paired phrases, shield with shield and spear with spear, convey the sound and mass of the clash.
The scales stand for fate. The Achaean pan sinking to earth shows their doom, while the Trojan pan rising shows their present success.
Diomed speaks courteously and practically to Nestor, showing his respect for age and his steady courage when others flee.
Diomed wishes the earth might swallow him rather than be shamed, though the shame is the cost of obeying Jove.
Hector mocks the Achaean wall, but readers know Jove's favour is temporary and that Hector will die before Troy is saved.
Hector addresses his horses by name as if they could understand, which shows his closeness to them and his pride.
Olympus is made to quake with Juno's rage, showing the goddess's anger is on a cosmic scale.
Ajax and Achilles are described as trusting their own strength, which sums up their proud, self-reliant nature.
Teucer darting back behind Ajax's shield is compared to a child running to its mother, conveying protection and dependence.
Calling Hector a "mad dog" shows Teucer's frustration and casts Hector as a ferocious, dangerous beast.
Gorgythion's drooping head is likened to a poppy heavy with spring rain, making his death tender and pitiable.
Hector is compared to a hound chasing a boar or lion, picking off the hindmost. It shows his relentless pursuit and the Achaeans' fear.
Minerva's bitter mention of Jove's pet name for her shows her hurt and resentment, and hints at a coming rebellion.
The gates of heaven bellow and open of their own accord, as if alive and obedient to the goddesses.
Iris repeats Jove's words almost exactly, as heralds do. This stresses that the threat is Jove's own and carries his full authority.
Olympus reeling beneath Jove as he sits conveys his overwhelming power and the tension among the gods.
The same darkness brings sorrow to the Trojans and relief to the Achaeans, a balanced antithesis showing the opposed sides.
Hector wishes he were as sure of immortality as of victory, yet the audience knows his confidence is misplaced and he will die.
The Trojans sacrifice with high hopes, but the gods who hate Troy refuse the offering, undercutting their confidence.
The long, calm night scene of stars and a glad shepherd is compared to the Trojan fires, giving a peaceful beauty that contrasts with the war to come.
